props.title: Rosewood

sections.content: Rosewood stands as one of cinema's most powerful depictions of racial violence in American history. Director John Singleton, fresh from groundbreaking works like Boyz n the Hood (1991), tackled the true story of a 1923 massacre in Florida where a white mob destroyed a prosperous Black community. The film's unflinching portrayal, anchored by Ving Rhames' commanding performance as the fictional Mann, weaves together historical fact with dramatic elements to illuminate a shamefully buried chapter of American history.

sections.content: Singleton's direction in Rosewood employs techniques that would influence later historical dramas about racial violence. Like Detroit (2017) and Judas and the Black Messiah (2021), he uses intimate camera work during peaceful scenes to establish community bonds, then switches to more chaotic, documentary-style footage during violent sequences. This approach creates an immediate, visceral connection to the horror while maintaining the humanity of the victims.

The film shares DNA with other pivotal works examining American racial violence, particularly Malcolm X (1992) and 4 Little Girls (1997). These films collectively form a crucial cinematic examination of how racial terrorism shaped 20th century America. Rosewood particularly excels in showing the economic motivations behind racial violence, a theme later explored in Tulsa Burning: The 1921 Race Massacre (2021). sections.content: Rosewood's influence can be seen in recent films like The Hate U Give (2018) and Queen & Slim (2019), which similarly explore the intersection of racial violence and community resistance. Its technique of blending historical accuracy with dramatic storytelling has become a template for films dealing with racial trauma, evident in works like Till (2022) and One Night in Miami (2020).
